title: God in all things
hook: Ignatian spirituality finds God in all things

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Suscipe, the prayer at the end of the Exercises that hands everything back. Your line was take, Lord, receive. Which one thing was hardest to hold out in open hands? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

A young Jesuit student sits at a desk with a grammar book open, and he is worried. He joined to pray, and now his days are full of verb endings and lecture notes. When does the real spiritual life begin? The answer Ignatius gives students like him is not a longer hour in the chapel. He tells them to seek the presence of God in everything: in conversation, in walking, in seeing, tasting, hearing, thinking, in all that they do. The grammar book is not the thing in the way. Today's phrase is the short form of that answer, and it runs under everything the Jesuits do next.
screen: `A STUDENT AND A GRAMMAR BOOK.` → `WHEN DOES THE REAL PRAYER START?` → `SEEK GOD IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: God in all things. Four words, and they can sound like a greeting card. In the Ignatian tradition they carry more weight. They grow straight out of the place the Exercises ended yesterday. In the Contemplation to Attain Love, Ignatius asks the retreatant to consider how God dwells in creatures: giving being to the elements, life to the plants, feeling to the animals, understanding to people. And then a step further: God works and labors in all created things on our behalf. So the world is not a stage set God left behind. It is a place where God is busy. Saint Paul says it to the crowd in Athens, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Ignatius takes that and makes it practical. In the guidance he wrote for Jesuits, he asks those who are studying, who can't spend long hours in formal prayer, to practice finding God in what is in front of them. A conversation can be a place of prayer. So can a walk, or a meal, or a page of hard reading. Two cautions keep this honest. First, it does not mean everything is God. Catholic teaching keeps the Creator and the creature distinct; God is present in things, not the same as them. Second, it does not mean everything that happens is good. Ignatius also wrote the rules for discernment, because some movements lead away from God. Finding God in all things is a habit of attention, not a pair of rose-colored glasses. In practice it might mean noticing the steam off a cup of coffee, a coworker's patience, a child's question, and asking quietly: where is God at work in this?
screen: `GOD DWELLS IN CREATURES.` · `GOD WORKS AND LABORS FOR US.` · `PRAYER IN A WALK, A MEAL, A PAGE.` · `NOT EVERYTHING IS GOD. NOT EVERYTHING IS GOOD.` · then, large: `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God in one ordinary thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing within reach or in view: a cup, a window, your own hand, a plant on the sill. Look at it as if for the first time. Notice its color, its weight, how it came to be here, who made it or grew it. Then ask, without forcing an answer: if God is at work in all things, how might God be at work in this one? If you pray, you can simply say thank you for it. If nothing comes, the looking itself is the practice. The bell holds the time.
God in all things. The Ignatian habit of looking for God's presence and work in ordinary life, in study and talk and meals, not only in church. Today's word.
Your line: all things. Today, pick one boring moment, washing a dish, waiting at a light, and say the line to yourself there. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In the Ignatian tradition, people practice finding God in all things by paying attention to daily work, conversation and study as places of prayer, often looking back over the day in the examen.

fork.setup: you're a young Jesuit student. your days are full of lectures and you have little time to pray. what does Ignatius tell you?
options: drop the studies and pray longer.
look for God's presence in the studies themselves.
wait until the studies are done to pray.
fork.reveal: he asks students to seek God in everything they do: talking, walking, seeing, thinking. the desk can be a place of prayer.
